lesson_title: Meanders and Oxbow Lakes: The River That Amputates Itself
hook_text: A river spends decades digging a loop — then one flood, and it cuts the whole loop off.
clip_script: Watch the neck — the narrow strip of land between the two limbs of the loop. With every flood, the outer-bank erosion on each side eats into that neck from both directions, and the neck narrows. The river is working towards its own shortcut. Then comes the flood that finishes it. In high flow the river breaks through the narrowed neck, and the water abandons the long way round. The old loop is cut off. Sediment settles at the two ends of the abandoned loop, plugging it off. What remains is a horseshoe of standing water beside the river — the oxbow lake.
visual_style: Time-lapse aerial of a meandering river, the loop tightening year by year, then a flood surge punching through the neck and the loop fading into a still horseshoe lake.
pacing: Slow build through the tightening loop, sudden break at the flood, calm landing on the lake.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own the eight-line oxbow paragraph before November.
